title: The Marrow That Walked Away
label: A Bizzing mystery
setting: the Story Garden, the Flower Show

card.text: It is Flower Show morning in the Story Garden. Grandpa Okoro's prize marrow, Big Bertha, has vanished from the show tent! A garden gnome sits in her place. One thin line runs away across the grass, with no footprints. Judging is at eleven. No marrow, no prize. A note says "she moved it". Who is she?

cutscene.picture: Already hot. The round window is propped open and the harbour smells of salt. The dumbwaiter rattles up. On the bun tray, instead of buns, a folded letter with soil on it.

cutscene.place: The Story Garden, ten past nine.
cutscene.picture: Heat shimmers over the gravel paths. Hedges, a striped show tent, bunting, bees, a brass band tuning up somewhere. The clock on the white bandstand says ten past nine. Grandpa Okoro waves both arms by the tent door.

lines.text: Judging is at eleven! No marrow on the table, no prize!

cutscene.picture: Hot yellow light through the canvas. A long table, a label holder with no label, and in the middle of a big empty space, a small garden gnome with a fishing rod, grinning.

lines.text: Big Bertha! Gone! And this… person in her place!

cutscene.place: The grass outside the tent door.
cutscene.picture: One thin line, pressed into the grass like a pencil mark, runs away from the door towards the gravel path, and stops. Not one footprint beside it. Dev on his knees.

lines.text: She walked away! Big Bertha walked away all by herself!
Hunches do not beep. Marrows do not walk. Read first.

cast.manner: warm, proud, in a hurry; reads too fast

cast.name: Mrs Hilda Pell

cast.manner: grumpy on the outside, kind underneath; says "Hmph"
cast.motive: Big Bertha might beat her Green Giant
cast.secret: the paper in her hat is a present, her secret compost recipe, written for Grandpa "in case you lose"

cast.name: Kip Mensah
cast.look: 7, a boy who loves pumpkins; gap-toothed, pumpkin-orange jumper, a toy trowel in his pocket
cast.manner: cheerful, honest, every answer is about pumpkins
cast.motive: he loves round green things and was seen carrying one
cast.secret: he held his small pumpkin up to Big Bertha, so it could see how big to grow

cast.motive: a vanished marrow would be the greatest prank in Gnome history
cast.secret: the Chief Gnome is scared of the dark, which is why gnomes only ever come at sunrise

cast.name: Sami Haddad
cast.look: the Story Garden's gardener (epilogue only); muddy boots, a pencil behind one ear

cast.name: the new detective
cast.manner: the one who marks, links and accuses

docs.title: Grandpa Okoro's letter
docs.author: Grandpa Okoro
docs.where: sent up by the bakery dumbwaiter
docs.picture: a letter on lined paper, soil fingerprints, a drawing of a very long marrow with a smile; the P.S. squeezed in sideways at the bottom
docs.body:
Dear detectives,
[[c:long|My long green marrow has gone]]!
[[c:says-she|The gardener's note says she moved it]].
It must be Mrs Pell!
Or that pumpkin boy, Kip.
[[c:round|He carried something round and green]].
[[c:barrow|P.S. My wheelbarrow is gone too!]]
— Grandpa Okoro

talk.text: I read the note. Very quickly. It is plain as day.
Footnote: a marrow is a giant courgette. Americans say zucchini. Footnote to the footnote: it just never stopped growing.
A wheelbarrow too! Two things gone!
Oh, the barrow. Somebody is always borrowing that. Bertha is what matters.
Plain as day is when we read most carefully. New detective, the note is pinned to the tent pole.

docs.title: The gardener's tent notes
docs.author: Sami Haddad, gardener
docs.picture: a page from a small spiral pad, pencil, a doodle of a sun with a frowning face, a tiny wheelbarrow
docs.body:
Tent notes, Friday. [[c:hot|Very hot!]]
[[c:pell-five|At five, Mrs Pell watered her roses]].
[[c:pell-she|She grumbled about the heat]].
[[c:zuri-six|At six, Zuri Okoro came with a wheelbarrow]].
[[c:she-moved|She moved the marrow in the evening]].
I went home at eight.
— Sami, gardener

talk.text: There! 'She moved the marrow.' And Mrs Pell is right there in the note. Hunch-o-meter: ten!
Two people in that note are a she, Nell.
…Nine.
Each she points back to someone. Who is named just before each one? Mark what you find.
Zuri Okoro? She's in my rowing club! She's in the long race this morning, right round the island. It finishes at half past ten.
My Zuri? She was only helping Sami, I expect. No, no. It is Hilda Pell. I know a cross face when I see one.
So we can't ask Zuri anything till half past ten.
Footnote: judging is at eleven. Footnote to the footnote: it is now nine fourteen.

docs.title: Flower Show Rules
docs.author: the Story Garden Show Committee
docs.where: painted board by the tent door
docs.picture: a wooden notice board on two legs, a carved oak leaf at the top, a row of vegetables carved along the bottom
docs.body:
Flower Show Rules
Judging is at eleven.
[[c:wilt|In the heat, vegetables wilt]].
[[c:droopy|They go soft and droopy]].
[[c:lose|A wilted marrow cannot win]].
[[c:shed|Spare pots go in the shed under the oak]].
[[c:cool|It is the coolest place in the garden]].

talk.text: The canvas creaks in the heat. A bee bumps against the tent roof, again and again, looking for a way out.
There's a shed under that oak. Door shut.
Footnote: an oak can live for hundreds of years. Footnote to the footnote: this one looks about a Tuesday old. Very small oak.
Small, but shady.

gloss.wilt: wilt: to go soft and droop, often in heat.

docs.title: The Show Catalogue
docs.author: the Show Committee
docs.where: a pile on the table by the door
docs.picture: a little folded booklet, a ribbon of green on the cover, a pressed daisy. Tucked inside the Class 4 page: a small cream card with one perfect ink blot.
docs.body:
Show Catalogue
Class 4: Biggest Marrow
Mrs Pell: Green Giant
Mr Okoro: Big Bertha
Class 5: Pumpkins
[[c:kip-entry|Kip Mensah, age 7: a small green pumpkin]]
Class 6: Best Garden Gnome
The Gnome Society: Gerald

talk.text: Footnote: a marrow is a kind of squash. Footnote to the footnote: so is a pumpkin. Big Bertha and Kip's pumpkin are cousins.
Another one. Same blot.

docs.title: the calling card
docs.author: B.
docs.where: tucked inside the Class 4 page of the Show Catalogue
docs.picture: a small cream card with one perfect ink blot
docs.body: Every gap has a word. — B.

docs.title: The note under Gerald
docs.author: the Garden Gnome Society
docs.where: under the gnome on Big Bertha's empty table
docs.picture: a paper cut in the shape of a pointed hat, red ink, a drawing of a gnome winking
docs.body:
Ha ha! The Gnomes were here!
[[c:sunrise|We came at sunrise, as always]].
[[c:line|Who drew that line on the grass? Not us!]]
[[c:never|We never touch the vegetables]].
That is Gnome Rule One.
— The Garden Gnome Society

talk.text: Pranksters! In the tent! Leaving notes! Hunch-o-meter—
Don't.
Chapter end. Dev turns the catalogue over in his hands, frowning.
That card. I read the Class 4 page when we came in. There was no card in it then.
Footnote: it smells of violets. Footnote to the footnote: there are no violets in this tent.
The tent flap lifts, and falls. Outside, the bunting hangs quite still. There is no wind at all.

docs.title: Mrs Pell: Did you move Grandpa Okoro's marrow?
docs.author: Mrs Hilda Pell
docs.picture: Mrs Pell's portrait on the bench under the bandstand: sun hat with a fierce brim, gardening gloves, watering can.
docs.body: Certainly not! Why would I touch his marrow? Mine is bigger. Well. Nearly.

docs.title: Mrs Pell: When were you in the tent?
docs.author: Mrs Hilda Pell
docs.picture: Mrs Pell's portrait on the bench under the bandstand: sun hat with a fierce brim, gardening gloves, watering can.
docs.body:
At five. I watered my roses.
[[c:pell-home|Then I went home for tea]].
I always have tea at half past five.

docs.title: Mrs Pell: What did you see?
docs.author: Mrs Hilda Pell
docs.picture: Mrs Pell's portrait on the bench under the bandstand: sun hat with a fierce brim, gardening gloves, watering can.
docs.body: His marrow, on its table. Long and green and showing off. I said "Hmph." It said nothing.

docs.title: Mrs Pell: Why are you so cross?
docs.author: Mrs Hilda Pell
docs.picture: Mrs Pell's portrait on the bench under the bandstand: sun hat with a fierce brim, gardening gloves, watering can.
docs.body:
I am always cross. It saves time.
Also, his marrow is very fine.
Do not tell him I said so.

docs.title: Mrs Pell: Where is your marrow?
docs.author: Mrs Hilda Pell
docs.picture: Mrs Pell's portrait on the bench under the bandstand: sun hat with a fierce brim, gardening gloves, watering can.
docs.body: On its table, by the door. Where marrows belong. Not walking about.

docs.title: Mrs Pell: What is that paper in your hat?
docs.author: Mrs Hilda Pell
docs.picture: Mrs Pell's portrait on the bench under the bandstand: sun hat with a fierce brim, gardening gloves, watering can.
docs.body:
Nothing! It is private.
[[c:pell-hat|It has his name on it]].
So what? Hmph.

docs.title: Mrs Pell: May we read the paper?
docs.author: Mrs Hilda Pell
docs.picture: Mrs Pell sitting very straight on the wall outside the gate, watering can on her knee, a folded paper in her gloved hand.
docs.body:
Oh, very well.
[[c:pell-gift|"For Emeka. My secret compost. In case you lose."]]
[[c:pell-tea|I wrote it at home, with my tea, at six]].
Hmph.

docs.title: Kip: What did you carry last night?
docs.author: Kip Mensah
docs.picture: Kip's portrait on the bench under the bandstand: gap-toothed, pumpkin-orange jumper, a toy trowel in his pocket.
docs.body: My pumpkin! It is small and round. It is green now. Pumpkins start green, you know.

docs.title: Kip: When were you in the tent?
docs.author: Kip Mensah
docs.picture: Kip's portrait on the bench under the bandstand: gap-toothed, pumpkin-orange jumper, a toy trowel in his pocket.
docs.body:
[[c:kip-six|At six, with Mum]].
I put my pumpkin on its mat. Mum said, "Home by half past."

docs.title: Kip: Did you see anyone else?
docs.author: Kip Mensah
docs.picture: Kip's portrait on the bench under the bandstand: gap-toothed, pumpkin-orange jumper, a toy trowel in his pocket.
docs.body:
[[c:kip-barrow|A big girl with a wheelbarrow]].
She looked at the long marrow.
[[c:kip-wilt|She said, "It will wilt in here!"]]

docs.title: Kip: What does wilt mean?
docs.author: Kip Mensah
docs.picture: Kip's portrait on the bench under the bandstand: gap-toothed, pumpkin-orange jumper, a toy trowel in his pocket.
docs.body: I don't know! I'm seven. I know *pumpkin*. I know *orange*. I know *very big*.

docs.title: Kip: Were you at Big Bertha's table?
docs.author: Kip Mensah
docs.picture: Kip's portrait on the bench under the bandstand: gap-toothed, pumpkin-orange jumper, a toy trowel in his pocket.
docs.body:
Um. Yes.
[[c:kip-show|I held my pumpkin up to the long marrow]].
It's a secret.
Please don't tell.

docs.title: Kip: Why do you love pumpkins?
docs.author: Kip Mensah
docs.picture: Kip's portrait on the bench under the bandstand: gap-toothed, pumpkin-orange jumper, a toy trowel in his pocket.
docs.body: They are round and happy. They sit very still. You can't lose a pumpkin.

docs.title: Mr Puddle: When were you in the tent?
docs.author: Mr Hamish Puddle, Chief Gnome
docs.picture: Mr Puddle's portrait on the bench under the bandstand: tall, thin, pointed red felt hat, false white beard on elastic.
docs.body: At sunrise. Gnomes are early. The dew was on our beards.

docs.title: Mr Puddle: What did you leave?
docs.author: Mr Hamish Puddle, Chief Gnome
docs.picture: Mr Puddle's portrait on the bench under the bandstand: tall, thin, pointed red felt hat, false white beard on elastic.
docs.body: One gnome in every tent. In the marrow tent, we left Gerald. He fishes.

docs.title: Mr Puddle: Where did you put Gerald?
docs.author: Mr Hamish Puddle, Chief Gnome
docs.picture: Mr Puddle's portrait on the bench under the bandstand: tall, thin, pointed red felt hat, false white beard on elastic.
docs.body:
[[c:empty|We put Gerald on the empty table]].
It looked lonely. Gerald cheers up a table.

docs.title: Mr Puddle: Did you take the marrow?
docs.author: Mr Hamish Puddle, Chief Gnome
docs.picture: Mr Puddle's portrait on the bench under the bandstand: tall, thin, pointed red felt hat, false white beard on elastic.
docs.body: Never! We never touch the vegetables. Gnome Rule One. Gnome Rule Two is: smile.

docs.title: Mr Puddle: Why do gnomes never come at night?
docs.author: Mr Hamish Puddle, Chief Gnome
docs.picture: Mr Puddle's portrait on the bench under the bandstand: tall, thin, pointed red felt hat, false white beard on elastic.
docs.body:
[[c:gnome-secret|That is a Gnome secret]].
Gnomes do not tell secrets.
Gnome Rule Three.

docs.title: Mr Puddle: Why do you play these jokes?
docs.author: Mr Hamish Puddle, Chief Gnome
docs.picture: Mr Puddle's portrait on the bench under the bandstand: tall, thin, pointed red felt hat, false white beard on elastic.
docs.body: To make people smile. Did you smile? A little? Then it worked.

chapter4Talk.text: At six, Mrs Pell was at home with her tea. At six, Zuri came with a wheelbarrow.

talk.text: Chapter end. Mrs Pell stands up from the bench and straightens her sun hat. A folded paper slides half out from under the brim. On the outside, in big, fierce letters: OKORO. She pushes it back in, quickly.
Did you see that?

deductions.label: who "she" is
deductions.statement: "She moved the marrow" means Zuri, not Mrs Pell. Zuri is the last girl named before that "she". Mrs Pell's own "she" is a sentence earlier, grumbling.
deductions.why: Grandpa read she and jumped to the person he was cross with. The pronoun points back to the nearest girl named: Zuri, who came with a wheelbarrow, which is what you need to move a marrow longer than Dev.
hints: There are two shes in the gardener's notes. Take them one at a time.
Who is named in the line just before 'She moved the marrow'?
Link 'At six, Zuri Okoro came…' to 'She moved the marrow…'.

deductions.label: meaning
deductions.statement: Zuri moved Big Bertha so she would not wilt in the hot tent, and the coolest place in the garden is the shed under the oak. That is where the marrow is.
deductions.why: Kip heard the word but did not know it. The rules board says what wilt means and what it costs: a wilted marrow cannot win. Zuri was not taking Big Bertha. She was saving her. And to stop a thing wilting in the heat, you take it somewhere cool.
hints: Kip heard a word he didn't know. Find it in another document.
What makes vegetables wilt? Where would you take one to stop it?
Link 'It will wilt in here!' to 'the coolest place in the garden'.

deductions.label: how the marrow walked
deductions.statement: The thin line in the grass was made by one wheel: a wheelbarrow. Grandpa's wheelbarrow went missing too, and Zuri came with a wheelbarrow.
deductions.why: It answers how could it? A wheelbarrow has one wheel, so it leaves one line. The grass was baked hard ("Very hot!"), so feet left no mark. A wheel carrying a marrow as heavy as Kip did.
hints: How many wheels made that line?
What has one wheel? Has anyone lost one?

redHerrings.note: Her she belongs to her own sentence, and a new girl is named before the marrow line. She was gone before six, writing a present at home. Secret: the paper in her hat is her compost recipe, for Grandpa.
Grandpa saw something round. Big Bertha is long. Kip was carrying his own pumpkin. Secret: he held it up to Bertha so it could see how big to grow.
The table was already empty, and the line already drawn, when the gnomes came. The marrow had gone the evening before. Secret: the Chief Gnome is scared of the dark.

talk.text: And I'll add one. Dawn: Zuri rows in the race. That's why she's not here.
Was the table full or empty when Gerald arrived? Show me the word.
Chapter end. Across the lake, a long horn, and then cheering.
Half past ten. The race is over. Zuri's coming in.
And Bertha's been somewhere since last night. In this heat.

events.text: Mrs Pell waters her roses, goes home, and writes Grandpa a note with her tea
Zuri arrives with a wheelbarrow; Kip brings his pumpkin
Zuri says it will wilt, and wheels the marrow away, leaving one thin line
The gnomes find the line, and leave Gerald on the empty table
Grandpa finds Gerald and writes to the agency
The race round the island finishes

accusation.question: Who moved the marrow, and where is it now?

place.prompt: Who moved the marrow, and where is it now?

wrongSuspect.pell: Read the gardener's notes again. Who is named just before 'She moved the marrow'?
wrongSuspect.kip: What shape did Grandpa see Kip carrying? What shape is Big Bertha?
wrongSuspect.gnomes: When did the gnomes come? And was Big Bertha's table full or empty?

accusation.weakEvidence: True. But does it show who moved it, or why? Pin the words that point to her, and the word that explains her.

reveal.text: Twenty minutes. New detective, the floor is yours.
Kip first. Grandpa saw him carry something round. Big Bertha is long.
It was my pumpkin! I held it up to Bertha, so it could see how big to grow.
Then I hope it was taking notes.
The gnomes came at sunrise. The table was empty, the line already drawn.
And we never come at night because… I am scared of the dark. There. A Chief Gnome.
Mrs Pell's she grumbled about the heat. Then she went home. At six, she was writing a present.
It was meant to be a secret. Hmph.
Now the deciding line. Grandpa, read your letter.
'The gardener's note says she moved it.'
And now Sami's note. Glasses on.
Grandpa pulls his glasses down and reads, slowly.
'At six, Zuri Okoro came with a wheelbarrow. She moved the marrow…' Oh. She is Zuri.
And the line with no footprints. One line means one wheel.
A wheelbarrow. Your wheelbarrow, Grandpa. It was there on the very first page.
And the grass was baked hard. 'Very hot!' Feet don't sink in. A wheel with Bertha in it does.
Zuri knew Bertha would wilt. So she took her to the coolest place in the garden.
The shed under the oak!
The bandstand clock: ten fifty.
Ten minutes! There's less minutes than ever!
Fewer minutes. Now, run!
The shed under the oak. Cool shade, a smell of moss, a slow drip. The door creaks open onto darkness.
Torch. My turn.
It was your turn last time.
Last time was a staircase. That doesn't count.
The torch clicks on. On damp sacks, beside a striped wheelbarrow, lies Big Bertha: long, green and perfectly firm.
Bertha! Oh, Bertha. You're cool as a cucumber.
Technically, sir, she's cooler. Cucumbers were in the tent.
Running feet. ZURI, plaits dripping, a medal bouncing.
Grandpa! I heard you across the lake! Bertha was going soft, so I wheeled her here. I asked Sami to write it down.
He did. I read it too fast.
He turns to the doorway.
Hilda. I am very sorry.
Hmph. I would have been cross too. It is a very fine marrow.
Nobody here did anything wrong. One small word was read in a hurry.
Zuri and Grandpa lift Big Bertha into the wheelbarrow together. Kip runs alongside, holding his pumpkin up so it can see.

epilogue.text: The show tent, eleven o'clock exactly. The judges in straw hats. Rosettes on a tray. Mrs Pell's name card is back on the Green Giant's table.
Mrs Pell's Green Giant wins first. Big Bertha wins second. Kip's pumpkin gets a special rosette: Most Hopeful Pumpkin. Kip holds it up to the pumpkin so it can see.
Mrs Pell presses the folded paper into Grandpa's hand.
My secret compost. Banana skins. Eggshells. And you say good morning to it.
You talk to your marrow?
Every day. Tell anyone and I'll deny it.
Grandpa pins his second-place rosette on Zuri. Zuri unpins it and gives it to the new detective.
You read the note properly. That's worth a rosette.
The rosette goes on the shelf, next to Admiral's white feather.
Sami the gardener pokes his head into the tent, pencil behind his ear.
Did someone read my notes?
Yes!
Nobody ever reads my notes.
Constable Tully arrives at last, ten minutes after the judging, holding an empty lead.
I came about a thief. Also, has anyone seen—
The Best Garden Gnome line-up: Gerald, a gnome with a wheelbarrow, a gnome with a lantern… and, sitting very, very still in a pointed red hat, a small brown fluffy dog.
We thought he was a new member.
The judges have pinned a rosette on him: Highly Commended.
Biscuit! He's never sat that still for me.
Nell, on the way home, stops The Comet by the harbour wall. She takes the folded form from her basket, writes Cases solved: 2 in the margin, looks at it, folds it again, and puts it back.

That evening, Felix borrows The Story Garden Guide from the little reading hut, to check his oak footnote. On the page about the oak, a painted sign reads: Keep off the grass, ______ the oak. A neat, empty gap, as if one word had been lifted out with tweezers.
The gap is five letters wide. I measured.
Every gap has a word. The card told us. Where have we seen a word about the oak today?
The child finds it in DOC 1.3, "the shed under the oak", and marks the single word. Ink runs from the notebook into the Blot Ledger. The first line of the Ledger reads: UNDER.
A word that vanished… and the case was hiding under the very same oak. Footnote: that is a coincidence. Footnote to the footnote: I do not believe it is a coincidence.

epilogue.direction: lifting the book to his nose, slowly
epilogue.text: Footnote to the footnote to the footnote: violets.
One word is not a sentence. Not yet.
Last panel: the reading hut at dusk, its door ajar. On the bench outside, where nobody was sitting a moment ago, a single violet petal.
Case solved. Skills used: who "she" means · a word's meaning · working out what isn't said. Blot Ledger: UNDER.

Heat shimmer over the gravel.
The tent door and the line: a close view of lawn, the grass slightly yellow and dry, one thin pressed line running away from the tent door to the edge of a gravel path. No footprints.
Inside the tent: long trestle tables of vegetables and flowers on cloths, hot yellow light through the canvas; one big empty space on a table with a small grinning gnome holding a fishing rod.
The shed under the oak: a young oak with a wide, low canopy; a little wooden shed in deep cool shade, moss on the roof; inside, clay pots stacked, damp sacks, a striped wheelbarrow, torchlight.
Bandstand interview corner: bench, bunting, flower boxes.
The reading hut at dusk: small, wooden, its door ajar; a bench outside; one violet petal on the bench.

art.notes: No lettering in any painting: the rules board, catalogue, gnome note, guidebook sign, Mrs Pell's paper and rosettes are painted blank; every word is set live (the OKORO on Mrs Pell's paper is live type laid over a blank fold). Document templates: lined letter with soil prints and a sideways P.S. (1.1), spiral-pad page (1.2), wooden notice board (1.3), folded catalogue booklet (1.4), hat-shaped red paper (1.5). Motion: heat shimmer, the tent flap lifting with no wind, the shed door creaking open, the torch beam, ink running into the Ledger; reduced motion: fades. Sound: bees, a brass band far off, a starting horn and cheering across the lake, the shed door, a slow drip. Silent under read-aloud.

Mrs Pell's secret: a present, not a plot

exercises.prompt: Welcome to the Training Desk! The note says: "At five, Mrs Pell watered her roses". Next: "She grumbled about the heat". Who is "She"?
exercises.explain: "She" points back to the last girl or woman named. The sentence before names Mrs Pell, so "She" is Mrs Pell. Kip and Grandpa would be "he".

exercises.prompt: The rules say: "In the heat, vegetables wilt". What does "wilt" mean?
exercises.explain: The very next line tells you: "They go soft and droopy." When a word is new, read the line after it. Writers often explain.

exercises.prompt: The rules talk about "vegetables" in the heat. Which is spelled right?
exercises.explain: Vegetables has four parts: veg-e-ta-bles. The middle "e" is easy to miss, so say all four parts slowly when you spell it.

exercises.prompt:
Grandpa writes: "My long green marrow has gone!"
What does the exclamation mark show?
options: He is asking the detectives something
exercises.explain: An exclamation mark shows a strong feeling, like surprise or upset. A question would end with "?". Speech marks would show someone else talking.

exercises.prompt: Use the tent notes and Kip's answers. Put these in order, first to last.
options: Kip put his pumpkin on its mat
answer: Kip put his pumpkin on its mat
exercises.explain: The times tell the order: Mrs Pell at five, Kip at six, and Sami went home at eight. Five, six, eight.

exercises.prompt: Mrs Pell says, "I am always cross". What does "cross" mean here?
exercises.explain: Cross has more than one meaning. Here Mrs Pell is talking about how she feels, so it means grumpy or annoyed.

exercises.prompt: Kip says pumpkins "are round and happy". Which part is a fact?
exercises.explain: You can check that a pumpkin is round. "Happy" is what Kip feels about pumpkins, so it is his opinion. A pumpkin cannot really be happy.

exercises.prompt: Case closed! Read: "At six, Zuri Okoro came with a wheelbarrow". Next: "She moved the marrow in the evening". Who is "She"?
exercises.explain: "She" points back to the last girl named. That is Zuri, in the line just before. Mrs Pell was named earlier, and Kip is a boy.

exercises.prompt:
Felix says a marrow is a giant courgette.
Grandpa's marrow is long and green.
What is a marrow?
exercises.explain: A marrow is a courgette that grew and grew. Americans call a courgette a zucchini. Careful: in America, marrow can also mean the soft middle of a bone. Same word, different meaning!

exercises.prompt: Grandpa writes: "The gardener's note says she moved it". What does the apostrophe in "gardener's" tell you?
options: The note belongs to the gardener
More than one gardener wrote it
A letter has been left out
exercises.answer: The note belongs to the gardener
exercises.explain: An apostrophe and s after a person shows that something belongs to them. The gardener's note is the note written by the gardener, Sami.

exercises.prompt: Sami signs the tent notes "Sami, gardener". The word is garden + -er. What does a gardener do?
exercises.explain: The ending -er can mean "a person who does this": a baker bakes, a teacher teaches, and a gardener works in a garden.

exercises.prompt: Grandpa says Kip "carried something round and green". The catalogue lists "a small green pumpkin". What did Kip most likely carry?
exercises.explain: Put the two documents together. Kip entered a small green pumpkin, and pumpkins are round. Round and green matches his pumpkin, not a long marrow.

exercises.prompt: Mrs Pell says the marrow was "Long and green and showing off". What does she mean?
options: It was dancing about on its table
It was really talking to Mrs Pell
exercises.explain: A marrow cannot really show off. Mrs Pell means it looked so good it seemed proud. She is a little jealous, and it makes us smile.

exercises.prompt: Mr Puddle says, "Gnomes are early. The dew was on our beards". Which word fills the gap? Gnomes are early, ___ the dew was on our beards.
exercises.explain: "So" joins a reason to what happened because of it. They came at sunrise, early, so the morning dew was still on their beards.

exercises.prompt: Kip came "At six, with Mum". Mum said, "Home by half past". What time did Mum mean?
exercises.explain: "Half past" on its own means half past the hour just talked about. Kip came at six, so Mum meant half past six.

exercises.prompt: The rules say the shed "is the coolest place in the garden". What does "coolest" mean here?
exercises.explain: Cool can mean "popular", but these rules are about heat. Here coolest means the least hot, which is why a marrow would not wilt there.

exercises.prompt:
Kip heard the girl say, "It will wilt in here!"
Why did Zuri move the marrow?
options: So she could enter it in the pumpkin class
So the gnomes could play a joke with it
exercises.explain: Zuri knew the tent was hot and a wilted marrow cannot win. She moved it to the cool shed to help Grandpa, not to take it.

exercises.prompt: Grandpa adds a line at the end: "P.S. My wheelbarrow is gone too!" What is a P.S.?
options: a line added after the end of a letter
the name of the person who wrote it
exercises.answer: a line added after the end of a letter
exercises.explain: P.S. is short for postscript, which means "written after". People add one when they remember something late. Read every P.S.: small lines at the bottom can matter a lot.

boardIntro.text: The bandstand clock says ten. Heat wobbles off the gravel like water.
Ten o'clock. One hour to judging.
And if Bertha's somewhere hot, she's wilting right now.

wrongLinks.quill: A name on a paper is not a marrow in a barrow. What does the paper say?

aside.text: Nell's hunch-o-meter hits ten for Mrs Pell; Grandpa calls for Constable Tully; Mrs Pell takes her name card off the Green Giant and walks out of the show.

lines.text: Hunch-o-meter: ten. Mrs Pell grumbled. Mrs Pell wants to win. And Mrs Pell has a paper with his name on it, hidden in her hat!
I knew it! Somebody fetch Constable Tully!
Kip runs off for the constable. Mrs Pell marches to the Green Giant's table and lifts off her own name card.
There. I am out of the show. A thief's marrow can't win, can it? Hmph.
Ten is a big number. Is it a true one?
The gate clicks shut behind her. On the bandstand, the clock says ten past ten.

aside.text: Clock: judging at eleven, no marrow no prize. Impossible thing: one thin line across the grass, no footprints (one wheel, grass baked hard). False solution: Mrs Pell, broken in chapter 4 by her paper. Hidden clue: Grandpa's P.S., his wheelbarrow is gone too. Escalation: Mrs Pell withdraws from the show. The Blot: a card that was not there a moment ago, smelling of violets.

revealSetting: The show tent, twenty to eleven. Hot canvas, the hum of bees. Mrs Pell by the door, her name card in her hand. Kip with his pumpkin. Mr Puddle with Gerald under his arm. Grandpa, glasses on his head. The new detective stands by the empty table.
